heading: Networks trained on the same task converge to the same algorithm
definition: networks trained on the same task converge to the same identifiable algorithm, rather than different algorithms depending on architecture and hyperparameters.
summary: Models trained on modular addition and sorting can learn different algorithms depending on architecture, initialization or seed, challenging the claim that all runs converge to the same algorithm. Independent groups find that related algorithms recur under specific conditions, while Pythia models of different sizes show broad consistency in their algorithms but differences in their components.

suggested_status.by_scale: Toy: C for unrestricted V6; recurrent algorithm families have substantial supporting evidence. <1B and 1–10B: ? for full V6, with coarse Pythia IOI consistency across scale. 10–100B and >100B: untested.
suggested_status.reason: The unrestricted statement is contested by architecture-dependent modular-addition computations (arXiv:2306.17844#r14, arXiv:2306.17844#r15) and seed-dependent sorting solutions with distinct ablation and length-generalization behavior (arXiv:2610.26974#r1, arXiv:2610.26974#r2, arXiv:2610.26974#r4, arXiv:2610.26974#r5). However, within each named strongly asymmetric-initialization or extreme-width condition (sigma2=0.013, sigma1=0.012, E=32, E=80), all evaluated sorting-model seeds select one solution class. This supports recurrence at the measured solution-class level; comparisons between conditions challenge unrestricted invariance (arXiv:2610.26974#r7, arXiv:2610.26974#r8, arXiv:2610.26974#r11, arXiv:2610.26974#r12). Recurrence of a qualified family remains supported by group-operation analyses (arXiv:2302.03025#r8, arXiv:2302.03025#r9). Larger-model evidence is narrower: Pythia IOI consistency concerns one family across sizes, with component differences (arXiv:2407.10827#R13). counts: versions.V6.verdicts.supports.studies = 26; versions.V6.verdicts.limits_scope.studies = 30; versions.V6.verdicts.challenges.studies = 6. These are the supplied script tallies, before the checked limits_scope-to-supports correction for the sorting study's within-condition recurrence. These categories overlap and are not independent replications. Scale coverage is given by versions.V6.studies_by_size; author-overlap uncertainty is recorded in versions.V6.tested_sharing_an_author_with_an_original.
suggested_status.open_questions: A result that could change the assessment would compare the same task across seeds, architectures and hyperparameters using a specified computational-equivalence criterion, causal interventions and OOD behavior, while including successful alternative solutions. At larger scales, comparable tests across independently trained model families are missing. Resolve whether Clock/Pizza disagreements concern computation or abstraction, and identify the currently unexplained seed outcomes.

source.title: Progress measures for grokking via mechanistic interpretability
source.authors: Neel Nanda; Lawrence Chan; Tom Lieberum; J. Smith; Jacob Steinhardt

original_result.setup: The study reverse-engineered one-layer transformers trained on addition modulo 113 using 30% of examples.
original_result.result: The main model used Fourier multiplication at five key frequencies; four other random seeds used the same algorithm with different frequencies. Across varied data fractions, depth, prime moduli, and regularization, every correctly generalizing model trained with weight decay reportedly implemented a variation of Fourier multiplication.
original_result.interpretation: This is the displayed original-result block, not a guarantee that the original tested every part of this claim.

sources.headline: MLPs and transformers learned the same group-operation algorithm family across tested groups and seeds.
Gradient descent and AdamW produced Fourier features with approximately the same phase relationship.
Learned modular-addition solutions largely factored into order-4 and order-6 Fourier families.
Two-layer encoders and decoders repeatedly learned the same modular carry algorithm.
Across tested Pythia sizes, the same three-step algorithm explained observed effects when identifying sentence recipients.
Group-operation models shared general representation properties, but the proposed detailed circuit fit only 55% of models.
Accurate addition models shared a circuit skeleton across seeds, digit lengths and training methods.
Grokking and gradual learning produced Fourier features of the same type, each using a single frequency.
Recurrent networks repeatedly learned the Fourier multiplication algorithm previously found in transformers.
MLP-Add, Pizza and Clock shared first-layer disc geometry and matching topology across depth.
Across depths, modular-addition MLPs retained first-layer Fourier features whose shapes deviated from pure sine waves.
Modular-addition models shared a proposed abstract template based on sinusoidal neurons.
GELU and ReLU MLPs concentrated their embeddings on shared Fourier frequencies to similar degrees.
Transformers repeatedly implemented the same three operations at predicted components.
Selected transformer heads showed consistent CMS across seeds without establishing algorithm identity.
Natural grokking and adding data for both reasoning steps recovered intermediate links through the same process.
Across seeds, Bellman-Ford shortest-path networks learned circuits with identical functions but different neurons.
Across activations and initializations, modular-addition MLPs repeatedly learned Fourier solutions that doubled the phase.
Rotating Dyck-3 bracket-matching representations across seeds gave accurate reconstruction and closely matching decoder features.
A fitted rotation enabled accurate readout transfer between modular-addition MLP seeds.
Successful LayerNorm and bounded models shared Fourier structure on modular arithmetic.
STRIDE embeddings shared the same peak frequency across six seeds.
Elliptic-curve rank transformers focused attention on prime numbers and represented the same mathematical quantity.
In a replication, an MLP learned the transformer's Fourier multiplication algorithm for modular addition.
Larger modular-addition MLPs learned the same algorithm as a small hand-built model.
Adding LayerNorm to the model preserved its modular-arithmetic algorithm.
Group-operation models selected different representations across seeds and architectures.
Parity subnetworks varied in size across seeds, while their algorithms were only hypothesized.
Group-multiplication models shared subgroup-based partitioning circuits but chose different subgroups across seeds.
Sparse modular-addition transformers learned attention heads that clustered inputs, with variants depending on initialization.
Modular-addition solution orders depended on task size and weight decay.
Architecture and training changed where addition models decided carries and how they made corrections.
Pythia sizes shared broad algorithmic steps but differed in attention-head use for detecting duplicate tokens.
Quantized transformers shared periodic frequency patterns; binary-weight models had noisier representations than the others.
Many group-operation runs did not fit the proposed circuit, and the deviations remained unexplained.
Accurate addition models varied in circuit details despite sharing the same core computational steps.
On Ising spin tasks, features varied across seeds; modular-addition feature locations depended on hyperparameters.
Group-operation models shared types of low-rank decomposition, but finer structure depended on initialization and architecture.
Modular-addition architectures differed in representation shapes, changes across layers and distribution statistics.
The shared sine-wave description masked architecture-dependent neuron shapes, frequencies and failed attempts to replace neurons.
Transformers and MLPs both used Fourier embeddings but learned different sets of frequencies.
Transformers shared an induction algorithm, but initialization determined which pair of layers implemented it.
Adding training data for the second reasoning step achieved comparable behavior through a different mechanism.
ReLU MLPs retained Fourier phase addition despite input weights shaped like square waves.
Rotating Dyck-3 bracket-matching representations left differences across seeds in causal effects and feature activation.
A mechanism based on discrete logarithms explained only about 80% of modular-multiplication seeds.
Modular-addition representations required rotational alignment for readout transfer across seeds.
Stronger weight decay weakened Fourier circuit coherence in bounded addition models.
Different fixed input orders led to different sets of frequencies in Fourier representations.
Elliptic-curve rank models differed substantially in attention strength and loss increases when interpolating raw weights.
Sorting seeds mostly converged to one solution type within particular initialization or width settings.
Modular-addition transformers shared cyclic operations but differed in rotation patterns and each pattern's repetition count.
During training, MLPs' and transformers' representations changed geometrically in opposite ways, without identified algorithmic differences.
Transformer seeds selected different frequencies despite using the same type of Fourier algorithm.
Modular-addition MLPs used broader frequency sets than the compared transformer.
With SoLU activations, neurons favored constant frequencies and departed from the usual Fourier explanation.
Modular-addition architectures and hyperparameters selected different algorithms, including algorithms not based on circles.
Modular-addition runs learned grid-shaped or circle-shaped representations, depending on seed and weight decay.
Initialization changed whether transformers learned inferential or symmetric solutions from identical training data.
GrokAlign's embedding proxy suggested a bias toward classification-style modular-addition solutions.
Sorting transformers learned different algorithms depending on seed, initialization and model settings.
Composition transformers learned lookup, sequential or hybrid solutions depending on training and seed.

untested.basis: arXiv:2606.15036#r2 reports matching broad solution structure, but the check for V6.against[16] specifies that detailed circuit analysis concerns the centroid model. Attention-strength differences and unaligned raw-weight barriers do not establish different algorithms; parameter symmetries can produce such barriers. untested.what: Convergence to the same identifiable algorithm across fixed-recipe one-layer ReLU (40,3)-parity runs.
untested.basis: arXiv:2303.11873#r9 measures active-subnetwork sizes through pruning. The checks correct its V6 state to cannot_determine and its V6 verdict to none: DNF-like implementations are speculative, and neuron counts establish neither algorithm identity nor algorithm diversity across runs.

wording_issues.issue: The records distinguish abstract algorithms, representations and circuit implementations. Shared geometry or Fourier features alone do not establish algorithm identity; different component placements alone do not establish different algorithms. In Dyck-3 transformers, SAE reconstruction transfer after Procrustes alignment fitted separately for each site and seed pair measures activation transfer, not algorithm identity; component-effect transfer and feature firing remain incomplete.

wording_issues.phrase: rather than different algorithms depending on architecture and hyperparameters
wording_issues.issue: Attention rate, width, depth and initialization change measured solution types in the modular-addition, sorting and anchor-function studies. Sorting solutions can recur across seeds within fixed strongly asymmetric initialization or extreme-width conditions; the challenge arises from changes between conditions. In anchor-function transformers, small initialization favors an inferential mapping, while larger, but not very large, initialization favors a symmetric mapping. These mechanistically distinct solutions challenge unrestricted algorithm invariance.

wording_issues.phrase: networks trained on the same task converge
wording_issues.issue: Task identity leaves consequential training choices unspecified. In relational transformers, second-hop-only augmentation yields comparable behavioral performance without the bridge-recovery path shared by natural and both-hop training, challenging mechanism invariance; the alternative mechanism is not identified. Loss schedules change sequential versus memorizing D3 computation. Example ordering changes modular-addition embedding frequencies while both orderings retain Fourier representations; this does not determine whether their complete algorithms are the same.

The original baseline identifies Fourier multiplication in its mainline model; that single-run identification does not establish convergence across runs. Separate comparisons in Appendix C.2 report Fourier-family agreement with differing key frequencies and frequency counts. Its generalization statement concerns generalizing weight-decay models, rather than identical solutions in every trained network.

Distinct embedding spectra, initialization-sensitive symmetric feature choices and high prediction agreement do not establish distinct or identical algorithms. The verdict fixes explicitly withhold algorithm conclusions from these proxies.

Some apparent universality results condition on successful or highly accurate models, use full-data training, or concern tasks without demonstrated grokking. A designed Bellman-Ford setup also restricts the available algorithm. These do not establish unrestricted convergence during grokking.

method_sensitivity.what: Attention rate and width shift the Pizza/Clock phase boundary; deeper modular-addition transformers often learn non-circular solutions. Fitted neuron descriptions also change with transformer depth: later layers require first-order and second-order terms or mixtures. In arXiv:2505.18266, Figure 7 replacement experiments use 1024 neurons per layer; Figure 8 uses two layers with 2048 neurons per layer. In fixed-recipe one-layer ReLU networks on (40,3)-parity, pruning-based analysis finds final active-subnetwork sizes {6, 6, 6, 8, 8} neurons across runs. Size variation establishes neither algorithm identity nor algorithm diversity.

Relative initialization scales, vocabulary size and embedding width change sorting solution types. Within each reported strongly asymmetric-initialization or extreme-width condition, all evaluated seeds select one solution class, supporting recurrence within that condition; comparisons between conditions challenge unrestricted invariance. On the anchor-function task, small initialization favors the inferential mapping, while large, but not very large, initialization favors the symmetric mapping. This initialization-dependent switch challenges V6.

Weight decay and modulus change mixtures of algebraic solution orders and types in modular-addition quadratic MLPs; multiple order-4/order-6 Fourier forms qualify convergence to one algorithm. Compressive modular-addition MLP regimes also reduce Fourier localization. In bounded-sphere modular-addition transformers, stronger decay reduces Fourier coherence, but FVE alone cannot determine algorithm identity. Successful configurations retain Fourier-based computation under frequency restriction; weaker coherence does not establish a different algorithm.

On addition modulo 9973 with the same task and architecture, STRIDE builds a Fourier representation rooted in F = 101; FIXED-RANDOM initially peaks at F = 2205 and finally at F = 3234. STRIDE retains peak F = 101 across the reported seeds, including stalled seed 555. These measurements establish ordering-dependent representation choices and cross-seed peak reproducibility; they cannot determine convergence to the same complete algorithm.

Answer-only versus full-sequence loss, curriculum and weight sharing change D3-composition algorithms. In relational training, natural and both-hop augmentation share bridge recovery. Second-hop full augmentation achieves comparable behavioral performance without that path; the study explicitly identifies a different underlying mechanism, challenging V6.

Fitted orthogonal alignment improves cross-seed readout transfer in modular-addition MLPs and SAE reconstruction transfer in Dyck-3 transformers. Dyck-3 Procrustes fits are separate for each site and seed pair; reconstruction transfer does not establish algorithm identity, and component-effect transfer and firing patterns remain incomplete. Raw-coordinate transfer failure and random-rotation controls do not establish different algorithms: V6 does not require identical coordinates. In fixed-recipe two-layer elliptic-curve rank classifiers across seeds, per-model prime/composite attention ratios range from 2.1–50× and unaligned raw-weight barriers from 0.18–0.89. These quantitative differences do not establish different algorithms; parameter symmetries can produce barriers between functionally equivalent models.

The informal activation exploration covers addition, subtraction and multiplication: SoLU is paired with LayerNorm, with weak constant-frequency preference and poor frequency explanations, especially for multiplication. The author attributes the poor explanations to departures from the Fourier algorithm; frequency preference alone cannot establish identity. Binary modular-addition transformers retain periodicity with noisier Fourier projections; ternary models retain periodicity with less noise than binary models. Neither identifies the exact algorithm conclusively. In a one-hidden-layer ReLU MLP trained with AdamW and weight decay 1.0, square-wave input weights retain the Fourier frequency/phase-sum mechanism; the cause of waveform differences remains open.

The geometry study assesses shared manifolds alongside differing diagnostic distributions. Separately, arXiv:2505.18266 states that common network-level aCRT structure can coexist with different circuit-level mechanisms; its batch-size comparisons change embedding distributions without identified significant differences in core learned structures. The verdict data for arXiv:2607.06628 and arXiv:2504.13292 treat embedding-spectrum differences and symmetric feature selection as insufficient to identify different algorithms. These are distinct assessments, not a reported within-study comparison of all diagnostics.

Seeds and architecture change selected irreducible representations, subgroup mixtures and group-word box covers within shared mathematical families. In the fixed-hyperparameter, one-hidden-layer S5 comparison, shared irrep sparsity and coset concentration establish common neuron properties. The detailed circuit explanation fits 55% of models, with a 91.7% mean accuracy lower bound for that explained subset; other runs have observed structural deviations. This limits uniform circuit identification without fully characterizing alternative algorithms.

In arXiv:2401.07993, carrying-over persists at (s, λ, dff) = (0.1, 0.2, 128), (0.3, 0.2, 1024), and (0.2, 1.0, 512), despite component reassignment. Three-layer models distribute carry decisions and retain a final carry MLP; perfect unablated accuracy is not explicitly reported. One s=0.1 run transfers previous-sum information in the first layer; priming alters MLP roles. The accurate arXiv:2402.02619 addition/mixed family spans 2–4 layers; head assignments, redundancy, timing and delivery routes vary. In three-layer, single-head attention-only induction transformers, initialization selects layer pairs (1,2), (1,3) or (2,3) implementing the same induction algorithm. Sparse-addition transformers occasionally generalize with unconventional clustering patterns within variations of the idealized circuit. Component placement alone does not demonstrate different algorithms.
